ai.literal: Having stayed and preserved, living in a home, all of it, is for the sake of cherishing guests and doing acts of benevolence.
ai.translation: The entire purpose of settling down and maintaining a domestic life is to welcome guests and perform acts of benevolence.
ai.modern: இல்லறத்தில் நிலைபெற்று வாழ்வதெல்லாம், விருந்தினர்களை உபசரித்து அவர்களுக்கு உதவி செய்வதற்காகவே ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the true purpose of a householder's life. The poet states that all the effort of settling down and maintaining a home is not for personal accumulation, but for welcoming guests and helping others. In classical Tamil, 'வேளாண்மை' means benevolence or helpful service rather than agriculture, which perfectly fits the theme of hospitality. Thus, domestic life finds its ultimate fulfillment in serving those who visit.

ai.literal: While a guest is outside, eating by oneself, even if it is the medicine of immortality, is not a thing to be desired.
ai.translation: Even if it is the nectar of immortality that prevents death, eating it alone while a guest is kept waiting outside is not a worthy thing to do.
ai.modern: விருந்தினர் வெளியே இருக்கும்போது, தான் மட்டும் தனியாக உண்பது, அது சாகா வரம் தரும் அமிழ்தமாகவே இருந்தாலும், விரும்பத்தக்கது அன்று.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the supreme value of hospitality. It argues that even if one possesses 'cāvā maruntu'—the legendary nectar of immortality that prevents death—it is improper to consume it alone while a guest is waiting outside. The key contrast is between 'viruntu' (guest) being outside ('puṟattatā') and 'tāṉ uṇṭal' (eating by oneself). By using the most precious substance imaginable as an example, the poet emphasizes that sharing food with others takes absolute precedence over one's own self-preservation.

ai.literal: The life of him who cherishes the arriving guest every day, suffering distress and going to ruin, does not exist.
ai.translation: The life of one who daily cherishes every guest that arrives will never suffer distress and fall into ruin.
ai.modern: தினமும் வரும் விருந்தினர்களை உபசரிப்பவனுடைய வாழ்க்கை, வறுமையால் துன்பப்பட்டு அழிந்துபோவது இல்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the material and spiritual security that comes from practicing hospitality. The poet asserts that a person who makes it a daily habit (வைகலும்) to welcome and care for guests will never experience poverty or ruin that causes them distress. The word 'பருவந்து' indicates the painful suffering that usually accompanies financial or personal downfall, which such a generous host is spared from. Thus, hospitality acts as a protective shield for one's livelihood.

ai.literal: With a pleased heart, the Goddess of Wealth will dwell in the home of him who, with a pleased face, cherishes a good guest.
ai.translation: The Goddess of Wealth will joyfully make her home with the one who welcomes worthy guests with a cheerful face.
ai.modern: முகமலர்ச்சியோடு நல்ல விருந்தினரை வரவேற்று உபசரிப்பவனுடைய வீட்டில், திருமகள் தன் மனம் மகிழ்ந்து வாழ்வாள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the immense reward of hospitality by drawing a beautiful parallel between the host and the goddess of wealth. The words 'அகன்' (heart) and 'முகன்' (face) are variants of 'அகம்' and 'முகம்'. When a host welcomes a guest with a cheerful face ('முகன் அமர்ந்து'), the goddess of wealth ('செய்யாள்') is so pleased that she resides in that home with a joyful heart ('அகன் அமர்ந்து'). The poet shows that outward warmth to guests invites divine, lasting prosperity into one's home.

ai.literal: Even seed sowing is it necessary indeed, of him who, having hosted guests, eats the remnant, the field?
ai.translation: Is it even necessary to sow seed in the field of one who eats only the remnants after hosting guests?
ai.modern: விருந்தினரை உபசரித்துவிட்டு எஞ்சிய உணவை உண்பவனுடைய நிலத்தில், விதை விதைக்கவும் வேண்டுமோ?
ai.explanation: This couplet uses a beautiful poetic hyperbole to praise the virtue of hospitality. It asks rhetorically if a farmer even needs to sow seeds in his field if he is someone who eats only the leftovers (மிச்சில்) after feeding his guests (விருந்து ஓம்பி). The word 'மிசைவான்' means 'he who eats', and 'புலம்' refers to his agricultural field. The poet suggests that nature itself will bless such a selfless host with effortless abundance, making the physical act of sowing seed redundant.

ai.literal: The departing guest having tended, the coming guest waiting for he who remains, a good guest to the heavenly ones.
ai.translation: He who hospitably sends off the departing guest and waits expectantly for the incoming guest will be welcomed as an honored guest by the gods of heaven.
ai.modern: செல்லும் விருந்தினரைப் பேணி, வரும் விருந்தினரை எதிர்பார்த்து காத்திருப்பவன், வானுலகில் வாழும் தேவர்களுக்கு நல்ல விருந்தினன் ஆவான்.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes the continuous nature of true hospitality. A virtuous householder does not merely host those who arrive, but actively cares for departing guests while eagerly anticipating the next ones. Such selfless dedication to others elevates the householder's character to a divine level. Ultimately, when they enter the heavenly realm, the celestial beings themselves will welcome them with the same high honor as a cherished guest.

ai.literal: There is no such thing as saying 'the benefit is of this much measure'; the benefit of the sacrifice of hospitality is of the measure of the guest's own worth.
ai.translation: There is no fixed measure for the benefit of hosting a guest; its true measure is the worth of the guest who is received.
ai.modern: "விருந்தினரை உபசரிப்பதால் கிடைக்கும் நன்மை இவ்வளவுதான்" என்று வரையறுத்துக் கூற முடியாது; அந்த விருந்தினரின் தகுதியே அந்த உபசரிப்பாகிய வேள்வியின் பயனின் அளவாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains that the spiritual and moral reward of hospitality cannot be measured by a fixed material standard, such as the cost of the food served. Instead, the true value of the act is determined by the character and qualities of the guest who receives it. The poet uses the word 'வேள்வி' (sacrifice) to describe the noble duty of hosting, elevating it to a sacred ritual. The word 'துணை' is repeated to emphasize that the measure of the reward matches the measure of the guest's worth.

ai.literal: Having strived and hoarded, 'we are destitute of support,' they will say—those who do not attain the sacrifice of hosting guests.
ai.translation: Those who fail to perform the sacrifice of hosting guests will later lament, 'We hoarded wealth with great pain, yet we are now left with nothing.'
ai.modern: விருந்தினர்களை உபசரித்து அந்த வேள்வியைச் செய்யாதவர்கள், 'நாங்கள் கஷ்டப்பட்டுச் சேர்த்துப் பாதுகாத்த செல்வத்தை இழந்து ஆதரவற்றவர் ஆனோம்' என்று பின்னாளில் வருந்துவார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the futility of hoarding wealth without using it for hospitality. The word 'parintu' indicates the pain and effort taken to accumulate wealth, and 'ōmpi' means guarding or hoarding it. Those who do not engage in the noble sacrifice ('vēḷvi') of hosting guests ('viruntu ōmpi') will eventually lose their wealth and lament that they have no support ('paṟṟu aṟṟēm'). The poet emphasizes that wealth not shared with guests is ultimately lost, leaving the hoarder destitute.

ai.literal: Within wealth, poverty is the folly of not practicing hospitality to guests, which exists with the foolish.
ai.translation: Poverty amidst wealth is the folly of not practicing hospitality to guests; such ignorance is found only among the foolish.
ai.modern: செல்வத்திற்குள் வறுமை என்பது விருந்தினரை உபசரிக்காத அறியாமை ஆகும்; இந்த அறியாமை அறிவற்ற மூடர்களிடம் மட்டுமே இருக்கும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet redefines poverty not as a lack of material wealth, but as the failure to share it. The poet states that possessing great wealth yet failing to practice hospitality is equivalent to being poor while rich. This failure is described as a form of ignorance or folly. Such foolish behavior is found only among those who lack true wisdom and understanding.

ai.literal: On smelling, will wither the Aniccham flower; face having changed, on looking, will wither the guest.
ai.translation: The delicate Aniccham flower withers merely by being smelled; likewise, a guest's heart withers the moment one's face changes and looks away.
ai.modern: அனிச்சப் பூ மோந்து பார்த்தாலே வாடிவிடும்; அதுபோல, முகம் வேறுபட்டுப் பார்ப்பதைக் கண்டவுடனேயே விருந்தினர் வாடிவிடுவர்.
ai.explanation: The poet compares the delicate nature of a guest to the legendary Aniccham flower. While the Aniccham flower is so sensitive that it withers merely upon being smelled, a guest is even more sensitive, drooping the moment they notice a cold change in the host's facial expression. This emphasizes that true hospitality is not just about providing food, but about maintaining a warm, welcoming countenance. Even a slight, silent shift in the host's face can deeply hurt a guest's feelings.
